item.content:encoded:
So, I'm not deep into the tale about SCP-590, but something about his part in this struck me as odd here, even though it might be a small detail. Maybe it's kind of unimportant and nitpicky, so I'll put it in a
spoiler.
spoiler.

The article says that SCP-321 was born in the 19th century, and that SCP-590 was used on her, which is possibly part of what led to her current state. Supposedly SCP-590 was used on her quite shortly after her birth, or at least before 1948 when work on her artificial heart started. However, SCP-590's photo, which is described as his appearance upon first arrival, looks as if the picture's from the.. 1970s, 80s? I'm bad at guessing time periods, so I could be off there… Either way, maybe I'm messed up with timelines here, but to me this now reads/looks as if SCP-590 was used at a time in which it was not in foundation custody. Maybe it's explained in the tales about these characters, but because I usually prefer only reading SCPs to reading tales, this stood out to me as an apparent mistake.

Other than that I thought this was a really intense and sad but intruiging read. I really love the last additions at the end. In such a quick and impersonal way, they show Adam's own journey up the ladder, as well as the merciless passing of time. It's quite heartbreaking that even as an O5 he's not able to do anything about her situation, as before that he could at least hold out hope that he would be able to change things as an O5. The last few sentences really elevated the article as a whole, for me.

item.content:encoded:
This is horrible. It almost seems like Adam kept on going up the ranks just to get his daughter back. Almost that he pushed himself to be able to go higher and higher, doing horrible, unethical tests, working himself to death, thinking that, if he became a higher rank, he could finally see his daughter, escape her from this prison she's in. But, only to find out that no matter how hard he works to get her back, his daughter's an anomaly no matter what, and nobody can get the foundation to make an exception to protocol and release an anomaly for no reason.

I think that there is a powerful message to this one; in the Foundation, no matter what your clearance level, no matter how far you go, no matter how hard you work, what importance you serve, …

you can't overthrow protocol.

Now, he's an 05, and he knows that he has built himself up for one reason, and that reason is gone now; to destroy the walls that separate him from her. He is stuck watching over the Foundation, the thing that is keeping his daughter locked up, treated like a thing and not a person. He cannot simply leave his post, for he is now a protector of the world, but he never wanted to be one; he just wanted his daughter, his family, his pride and joy, back in his arms.

+1. +1 all the way.

item.title: Legume
item.content:encoded: This reminds me of Anton's Key in the Ender's Shadow series by Orson Scott Card. Only, Anton's Key activates extreme intellect and memory capabilities of those whose genomes were altered with it, as well as the uncontrollable constant growth exhibited by SCP-321. An interesting notion to have a different trade-off of physical invulnerability versus abnormally low intellect. Upvoted!

FMA's theme is that of rising FROM tragedy and making the best of things.

321's theme is that from some tragedies, there is no rising.

The stories are entirely different on every level but the least relevant.

You don't have to like the story, but reducing a very well crafted article with a phenomenal, emotive story whose prose is efficient unto the point of poetry to a one-sentence description consisting entirely of reference to another, completely different work is insulting- and I didn't even write the article. They didn't pull it off better because they weren't doing the same thing.

I think that's what Azzleflux was getting at.
